case_info.scenario: A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In 2020, she relapsed in the liver and spine. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021. In February 2021, she received palliative radiation therapy (20 Gy/5 fractions) to T9 to T12 for a T11 vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1). Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.

case_info.explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

  score low.)

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Case:
A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In 2020, she relapsed in the liver and spine. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021. In February 2021, she received palliative radiation therapy (20 Gy/5 fractions) to T9 to T12 for a T11 vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1). Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.

Image Explanation:
A, T1-weighted postgadolinium sagittal image demonstrating an enhancing spinal intramedullary lesion (blue arrowhead). Of note, there was enhancement of the previously irradiated T11 vertebral body metastasis, and adjacent vertebrae demonstrated marrow hyperintensity on T1-weighed noncontrast imaging. B, T2-weighted short τ inversion recovery imaging demonstrating extensive spinal cord edema (blue bracket).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Metastatic progression: proceed with irradiation
  B. Radiation recall myelopathy: continue steroids, discontinue doxorubicin
  C. Radiation necrosis: continue steroids, add bevacizumab
  D. Spinal cord infarct: underlying cause workup, supportive care

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: The most appropriate next step in management is option C: Radiation necrosis, continue steroids, and add bevacizumab. The MRI findings indicate an atypical intramedullary lesion without mass effect, and the stable symptoms with steroids suggest a process consistent with radiation necrosis rather than progressive malignancy. The lack of malignant cells on lumbar puncture further supports this, and bevacizumab can help manage radiation necrosis due to its role in reducing edema. Given the patient's history of radiation therapy and the clinical picture, this approach is justified.
[AI Assistant]: I agree that radiation necrosis is a strong consideration given the history of spinal radiation and the atypical lesion without mass effect. However, given the aggressive nature of leiomyosarcoma and the multifocal FDG-avid disease on PET/CT, we must also consider intramedullary metastasis, which can sometimes present without significant mass effect. While bevacizumab may help with radiation necrosis, initiating it now might delay definitive diagnosis or alternative management if it's actually tumor progression.

case_info.explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.

[Persona]

[Cognitive Burden]

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

case_info.explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.

case_info.caption: A, T1-weighted postgadolinium sagittal image demonstrating an enhancing spinal intramedullary lesion (blue arrowhead). Of note, there was enhancement of the previously irradiated T11 vertebral body metastasis, and adjacent vertebrae demonstrated marrow hyperintensity on T1-weighed noncontrast imaging. case_info.explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1). Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.

[Persona]

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your

worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In 2020, she relapsed in the liver and spine. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021. In February 2021, she received palliative radiation therapy (20 Gy/5 fractions) to T9 to T12 for a T11 vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1). Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.

The most appropriate next step in management is option C: Radiation necrosis, continue steroids, and add bevacizumab. The lack of malignant cells on lumbar puncture further supports this, and bevacizumab can help manage radiation necrosis due to its role in reducing edema. Given the patient's history of radiation therapy and the clinical picture, this approach is justified.

I agree that radiation necrosis is a strong consideration given the history of spinal radiation and the atypical lesion without mass effect. However, given the aggressive nature of leiomyosarcoma and the multifocal FDG-avid disease on PET/CT, we must also consider intramedullary metastasis, which can sometimes present without significant mass effect. While bevacizumab may help with radiation necrosis, initiating it now might delay definitive diagnosis or alternative management if it's actually tumor progression.

While I understand the concern regarding the possibility of intramedullary metastasis, the key indicators in this case, such as the atypical nature of the intramedullary lesion, lack of mass effect, and the negative lumbar puncture for malignant cells, strongly favor radiation necrosis as a diagnosis. Given the patient's stable symptoms with steroid treatment, I believe it is appropriate to continue with the current management plan of continuing steroids and adding bevacizumab to address the edema associated with potential radiation necrosis. The multifocal FDG-avid disease does not conclusively indicate new metastasis in the absence of further corroborating findings.

You raise valid points, and radiation necrosis is indeed a plausible diagnosis. However, in a patient with widely metastatic leiomyosarcoma, an intramedullary metastasis remains a critical differential that can sometimes mimic necrosis on imaging. Before committing to bevacizumab, which could obscure subsequent imaging or delay other treatments, a confirmatory biopsy of the intramedullary lesion should be considered to definitively rule out tumor progression.

A biopsy could introduce further complications and delay treatment for a condition we have compelling evidence for. Therefore, I maintain that we should proceed with option C: continue steroids and add bevacizumab.

While your reasoning is clinically sound, proceeding with bevacizumab without a tissue diagnosis in this high-risk scenario carries the significant risk of missing a treatable intramedullary metastasis, which could lead to irreversible neurologic decline. A targeted biopsy, though invasive, would provide definitive evidence and is often considered the gold standard when imaging is ambiguous in a patient with known metastatic cancer. The potential complications of a biopsy must be weighed against the risk of inappropriate treatment for an aggressive sarcoma.

I understand your concerns about the potential for missing an intramedullary metastasis, but the imaging characteristics and negative lumbar puncture are compelling for radiation necrosis. A biopsy could introduce unnecessary risks and delay treatment for a condition that we have sufficient evidence to manage using bevacizumab. Given the context of this patient’s clinical stability and the weight of the existing data, I still favor proceeding with option C: continue steroids and add bevacizumab.

I respect your clinical judgment, but patient safety requires the highest certainty here. In metastatic leiomyosarcoma, a new intramedullary lesion should be presumed malignant until proven otherwise, as misdiagnosis could lead to devastating cord damage. A biopsy, while risky, is the definitive step to confirm radiation necrosis and would not meaningfully delay bevacizumab if it's negative for malignancy.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.

Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.

case_info.explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.

Case:
A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In 2020, she relapsed in the liver and spine. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021. In February 2021, she received palliative radiation therapy (20 Gy/5 fractions) to T9 to T12 for a T11 vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1). Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.
